title: Urban design and adolescent mental health: A qualitative examination of adolescent emotional responses to pedestrian- and transit-oriented design and cognitive architecture concepts
research_focus: To qualitatively explore, via go-along interviews, the in situ emotions of adolescents in response to specific urban design qualities (Pedestrian- and Transit-Oriented Design: imageability, enclosure, scale, transparency, complexity) and architectural concepts (Cognitive Architecture: biophilic architecture, symmetries, fractals), and to explore potential gender differences in these responses.

sample_context.description: 23 adolescents (ages 9-17, average 12.7 years; 12 boys, 10 girls, 1 non-binary) recruited through social networks and local youth organizations. Predominantly White/European (19 participants).
sample_context.setting: A medium-sized Canadian urban area (Kitchener, Ontario) along a predetermined 2.65 km route including an urban trail, residential street, urban bluespace, urban greenspace, public transit hub, and downtown street.

findings.antecedent: Natural reference points (bluespace/lake, greenspace/open field) and natural aural elements (flowing water, birds chirping, calm breeze)
findings.consequent: Creative, relaxing, inviting feelings; calming; restoring attention; lowered mental demand
findings.description: Nature-based reference points and sounds were connected by participants to creative, relaxing, and inviting feelings, enhancing intimacy and focus, and aiding in attention restoration.
supporting_quotes: It's calming. I can hear the water going around, I can see the ducks swimming around. I think that's a nice thing to look at or experience.
you can just focus on one thing

findings.antecedent: Non-rectangular buildings (round clock tower), historic character (pre-WWII architecture), and outdoor dining areas (local outdoor patio restaurant)
findings.consequent: Comfort, interest, welcoming feeling, fun social/leisure activities, positive reference point for navigation, distinctive designs
findings.source: 3.1.2. Non-rectangular buildings, historic character, outdoor dining
findings.theme_name: Non-rectangular buildings, historic character, outdoor dining
findings.description: Distinctive designs and social opportunities evoked comfort, interest, and a welcoming atmosphere, also serving as navigation points.
supporting_quotes: I would say relaxed [...] because of the clock tower because that's like a great checkpoint for stuff [...]
I like how all the houses are unique in their own way.

findings.antecedent: Artificial (mechanical) noise from cars, buses, and construction
findings.consequent: Annoyance, discomfort, emotional draining, uncomfortable, overwhelming, anxious feelings, mentally fatiguing, increased negative arousal
findings.description: Noise pollution from vehicles and construction led to annoyance, discomfort, and increased negative arousal, particularly for boys.
supporting_quotes: more uncomfortable
more overwhelming
cars come by here all of the time and it's not nice.
a little bit too much

findings.antecedent: Natural enclosure (tall trees, side hill, fences with natural accents like ivy/vines) in trail, greenspace, and bluespace areas
findings.consequent: Calming, restorative influence, enhanced intimacy, focus on focal point, present-moment awareness, safe feelings
findings.description: Tall trees and natural elements created a sense of intimacy, reduced external distractions, and fostered calm, restorative, and safe feelings.
supporting_quotes: I like how it's just a lake, there's nothing else distracting from it, when you come here you can just focus on the lake [...]
The giant trees just make you feel like you are submerged into the nature [...]

findings.antecedent: Built enclosure (tall buildings) in commercial street area
findings.consequent: Mixed responses: excited (positive) vs. uneasy/anxious/trapped/locked in (negative)
findings.description: Tall buildings elicited mixed emotional responses, with some finding them exciting and attention-grabbing, while others felt anxious, trapped, or closed in.
supporting_quotes: I kind of like it. I like being in the canyon of the buildings [...] it's cool
I feel, I guess, trapped [...] maybe kind of locked in here

findings.antecedent: Area furniture (benches, sidewalk barriers/metal posts, planters/flower boxes, street trees) and residential front yard gardens
findings.consequent: Inviting, comfortable, safe, refuge, mental/leisure 'breaks', social opportunities, welcoming feelings
findings.source: 3.3.1. Safety, natural, social, and accessibility of area furniture
findings.theme_name: Safety, natural, social, and accessibility of area furniture
findings.description: Human-scale features like street furniture and gardens provided safety, comfort, social opportunities, and mental breaks, particularly valued by girls.
supporting_quotes: It [street trees] almost makes me feel safe and it's really an attraction for your eyes like [...] 'Oh but there's those really cool plants! Or like gorgeous flowers. Or trees' [...]
instead there's plants and stuff that draw your eyes to them.

findings.antecedent: Mess/debris (broken sticks, overgrown weeds, litter) and perceived lack of area safety features (narrow sidewalk, lack of vertical barriers)
findings.consequent: Discomfort, reduced engagement with nature, uneasy, stressed, drained attention, increased negative arousal
findings.description: Mess and perceived lack of safety features led to discomfort, stress, and reduced engagement, particularly for girls.
supporting_quotes: a little bit guilty" because she was "trying to focus on the beauty of nature and then there's the garbage"
unsettled" and "stressed

findings.antecedent: Façades with windows and high density active uses (street accessible shops, restaurants)
findings.consequent: Safer, inviting, comprehensive evaluation of areas, happy, stimulated, inspired feelings of engagement
findings.source: 3.4.1. Façades with windows, high density active uses
findings.theme_name: Façades with windows, high density active uses
findings.description: Transparent façades and active uses created safer, inviting, and engaging environments, allowing for better evaluation of surroundings. Girls preferred windows, boys preferred active uses.
supporting_quotes: make [buildings] pop [...] more interesting [...] more inviting and makes people actually want to go in because they can see what's going on inside
think about what people are doing in the shops [...] it's pretty cool to think about all of the different stuff around

findings.antecedent: Façades lacking significant window presence and landscapes dominated by concrete
findings.consequent: Unwelcome, uneasy, anxious, nervous, uninteresting, chilling dynamic, unhappy, boring, unwelcoming, reduced desire to linger
findings.description: Windowless façades and concrete-dominated landscapes created unwelcome, uneasy, and boring environments, limiting engagement.
supporting_quotes: walking in a street that's pretty narrow and just concrete walls, I think you feel a little anxious, nervous, not the happiest
it's kind of closed off because there's really not that many windows [...] It feels like it's not very welcoming

findings.antecedent: Building façades with varied colours, designs, features (window patterns), and natural accents (ivy/vines)
findings.consequent: Attractive, interesting, improved character/quality, unique, happy, stimulated, inspired feelings of engagement
findings.description: Visually rich façades with varied colours, designs, and natural accents were perceived as attractive, interesting, and unique, fostering engagement.
supporting_quotes: I like how there is two triangles [pattern] in the middle [of the windows ...] that sticks out a lot. It looks good
I think it makes the street unique. If all the houses were the same colour or exactly the same, it would be kind of boring.

findings.antecedent: Worn-out façades/storefronts and landscapes dominated by grey
findings.consequent: Unwelcoming, unattractive, suspicious, creeped out, unhappy, monotone, boring, unwelcoming, increased negative arousal
findings.description: Worn-out façades and grey-dominated landscapes were perceived as unwelcoming, unattractive, and boring, leading to negative arousal.
supporting_quotes: [the restaurant's front is] worn-out, it almost looks like it's suspicious to me, like there's something going on behind it
I feel creeped out by that [house and porch] because the stairs don't look pleasant because they're dirty

findings.antecedent: Urban garden (enclosure by trees, varied flower colours), public art sculptures, info plaques
findings.consequent: Being away, relaxed, cheerful, calm, peacefulness, present-moment awareness, restorative opportunities. Mixed responses for non-natural features (welcoming vs. distracting). Girls emphasized calmness.
findings.description: Urban gardens with natural enclosure and varied colors fostered relaxation, cheerfulness, and present-moment awareness, especially for girls. Non-natural features had mixed reception.
supporting_quotes: I really like how it's arranged because [...] the trees block out some of the other stuff. It brings your attention into some of the smaller details inside the space.
something to look at and enjoy

findings.consequent: Calm, content, pleasing, complete, predictable, easy to process, positive attentional/emotional changes
findings.description: Symmetrical architectural designs were perceived as complete, predictable, and easy to process, leading to calm and content feelings.
supporting_quotes: It's pleasing to look at. And, you know what, I think that my mind was enjoying the symmetry without even acknowledging it because that was not something that came to mind.
[the symmetrical design] just makes me feel like 'okay this is a place to calm my mind' instead of it going super crazy

findings.consequent: Authenticity, creativity, flow, drawn in, interest, positive attentional impacts, reminds of nature (snowflake, flower, stars)
findings.description: Intricate fractal patterns in architecture were linked to feelings of authenticity, creativity, and flow, capturing attention and piquing interest, often reminding participants of natural forms.
supporting_quotes: It's kind of like something that draws you in and you want to sit and look at it, whereas everything else there's nothing special about it [...]
kind of reminds me of a snowflake or a flower [...] I like that feeling

derived_hypotheses: Future quantitative study examining the strength and generalizability of relationships between natural imageability/enclosure designs and adolescent mental health is merited.
Focused investigation into the role of culture in adolescent urban landscape perceptions is warranted.
Further exploration of human scale designs across different urbanicity levels (e.g., high density metropolitan, rural) could outline how they support or diminish adolescent mental health.

Relationships between CA concepts (e.g., curvilinear designs, floral ornamentation fractals) and adolescent emotional responses should be studied further, including comparisons to competing design paradigms.
More study is encouraged into the potential role that gender plays in the relationship between adolescent mental health and urban design.
mechanism_candidates: Natural imageability and enclosure designs offer adolescents more opportunities for comfort and positive emotional engagement by facilitating focus on restorative views and mitigating distractions.
Visual richness (complexity), high densities of active uses, and transparent façades contribute to creating meaningful experiences and improved perceived safety.
Human scale in design, particularly through safety and social features, facilitates environmental affordance actualization for mental breaks and leisure opportunities.
Predictability of symmetries satisfies visual preferences.
Attractiveness of fractal patterns captures attention and focus.
CA principles, broadly, help to foster more intimate person-place connections.
transferability_limits: Findings are limited by the cultural context (Canadian/Western) and socio-economic perspectives (middle to upper-middle class).
Participants were familiar with low-density urban designs and auto-oriented infrastructure, limiting generalizability to other urban forms.
Limited heterogeneity in social identities (e.g., non-binary, class, racial identities) restricts broader applicability.
The sample's concentration in the 10-14 age range limits age-specific analyses and insights for other adolescent subgroups.
The study focused on a relatively healthy group of adolescents, thus not providing insights into how those with internalizing/externalizing disorders or phobias experience these designs.
Data collection during warmer summer weather may have framed and limited emotional responses, suggesting potential seasonal effects.
The study's scale and specific route settings mean findings may not apply to rural, remote, peri-urban, or metropolitan/central business district environments.
limitations: Findings are limited by relevant cultural conditions (Canadian/Western, middle to upper-middle class perspectives).
Participants were familiar with low-density urban designs and auto-oriented infrastructure.
Limited heterogeneity in social identities (e.g., non-binary, class, racial identities).
Sample concentrated between ages 10-14, limiting age-specific analyses.
Study only evaluated healthy adolescents, not those with internalizing/externalizing disorders or other conditions.
Interviews conducted in warmer summer weather, potentially limiting emotional responses to a multi-season study.
Scale of the study limits applicability to rural, remote, peri-urban, or metropolitan/central business district environments.
